data.title: Snorkel AI's $350M Funding Highlights Industry Shift Toward AI Data Solutions
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation in a Series E led by Insight Partners and S32. The company's annualized revenue run rate reached $375 million, an 18-fold increase, as it expands from data labeling to data-as-a-service.
data.author: Win Warfield
data.full_text: Snorkel AI has raised $350 million in new funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, a jump that reflects how quickly demand for high-quality AI training data has intensified across the industry, according to TechCrunch, and a company announcement from co-founder and CEO Alex Ratner. The Series E round was led by New York’s Insight Partners and S32, formerly known as Section 32, with backing from existing investors including Addition, Lightspeed, Greylock, GV and Wells Fargo. The new valuation is nearly triple the $1.3 billion mark Snorkel reached 17 months ago when it raised a $100 million Series D, underscoring how rapidly investor enthusiasm has shifted toward companies selling the infrastructure behind AI models. Founded from research at a Stanford AI lab, Snorkel launched commercially in 2019 after four years of development. What began as a niche tool for making data labeling more efficient has evolved into a larger bet that the most valuable layer in AI may not just be models, but the data pipelines that feed them. Besides Ratner, the other co-founders of Snorkel AI are Christopher Ré, Paroma Varma, Braden Hancock and Henry Ehrenberg. Ratner completed his Ph.D. at Stanford University and is also an affiliate assistant professor at the University of Washington. Snorkel originally built software to automate data labeling, but the company has since moved into a broader business it describes as data-as-a-service. Instead of selling only tools for humans to label examples, it now delivers finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments that are assembled through a mix of software, synthetic data generation and subject matter experts. That approach is designed to serve frontier labs, hyperscalers, enterprise customers, vertical AI companies and U.S. government agencies, Ratner said in the company’s announcement. The company said its annualized revenue run rate has reached $375 million, an 18-fold increase over the past year. That growth mirrors a wider boom in the market for AI data providers, as model developers seek more specialized, higher-quality training material to improve performance in increasingly competitive systems. Other startups in the space have also reported striking growth. Mercor said its gross annualized revenue has climbed to $2 billion, Handshake reached $1 billion earlier this year and TechCrunch reported that Micro1 had scaled to $500 million. Those figures, however, do not all mean the same thing. Several of these companies reportedly pay a large share of revenue to the experts doing the work, which means gross revenue can overstate the economic value retained by the business. Snorkel argues its model is different because the payments it makes to experts are reflected in cost of goods sold rather than in the headline annualized revenue figure. That distinction matters for investors comparing fast-growing AI data businesses, particularly as the market expands beyond simple labeling toward more complex products such as finished datasets and simulated environments. 保険の引受審査を任せるなら、申請書類を読み、社内規程に照らし、必要な追加情報を取りに行き、最後に判断根拠まで書かせる必要がある。どの手順が正しく、どこで間違えたのかを判定できる基準がなければ、そもそも訓練も評価もできない。

Snorkel AI が提供するのは、その「作り方」ごと請け負うサービスだ。ツールを売って顧客に使ってもらうのではなく、専門家が関与してデータセット、ベンチマーク、評価、環境そのものを構築して納品する形態をとり、研究チームが定義した非独占のデータセットや環境を「Snorkel Data Series」として提供し、四半期ごとに更新すると案内している。
同社は、良いデータは集めるものではなく作るものだと表現する。具体的には、対象分野の専門家の知見に、タスク設計、プログラムによる自動チェック、校正された専門家レビュー、評価環境を組み合わせ、学習に使える測定可能なシグナルへと変換する。まずモデルがどこで失敗するかを評価し、その失敗に合わせてデータや環境を作り、また評価する。そうした反復を回す運用だと述べている。
分かりやすいのが「Enterprise environments」と呼ぶ製品群だ。企業の実際の業務フローを高い忠実度で再現した模擬環境の中で、AI エージェントに仕事をさせ、訓練と評価を行う。保険の引受審査を再現した環境では、一度目の試行で正解にたどり着けた割合（pass@1）が10.9%から42.0%へ改善したと同社は自社の計測結果として示している。

data.author: Camila Nogueira
data.full_text:
Share

CEO Alex Ratner said Snorkel AI has closed $350 million in new funding, putting the company's valuation at $3.5 billion as demand from frontier AI labs for increasingly complex training data and simulated environments accelerates. Insight Partners and S32 led the round, and existing backers Addition, Greylock and Wells Fargo also took part. Annualized revenue run-rate at the company now stands above $350 million, compared with roughly $20 million twelve months prior. That new figure is close to triple the $1.3 billion valuation Snorkel carried after its $100 million Series D round in May 2025, a raise that also debuted Snorkel Evaluate alongside an expert data-as-a-service product. Growth remains the priority for now, though Snorkel anticipates turning profitable this year. Plans for the new capital include hiring additional researchers and engineers, scaling up enterprise and government work, and building third-party AI evaluation services, plus expansion into fresh verticals and data categories. The company traces back to 2019, when a group of researchers exited Stanford's AI lab to start it. Snorkel initially sold software for labeling and managing training data before moving toward direct delivery of finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, a data-as-a-service line it opened in September 2025. Tens of thousands of specialists across disciplines such as coding, law and medicine make up Snorkel's network, and the company charges for the finished data products this group produces instead of billing hours worked. Ratner said the approach means contributors get paid more generously while margins stay protected. Coding data currently outpaces other categories in demand at the company. Snorkel refers to its offering as an "agentic data development platform," combining human specialists with thousands of purpose-built AI models and agents to construct and verify data quality. Specialists handle the design work, setting scenarios, tasks and grading rubrics, and automated systems take on most of the intensive review labor. Frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, enterprises and the U.S. federal government are among Snorkel's customers, the company said. On the balance between human and automated work, Ratner said human involvement isn't disappearing anytime soon, noting that all the data labs draw real value from will still carry some human input for the foreseeable future, even as the volume of that data increasingly depends on synthetic and automated methods to keep pace with rising complexity. S32 partner Andy Harrison, who co-led the funding round, summed up the shift: "Data is becoming more rare, more specialized, more difficult to find." This funding lands within a wave of investment that followed Meta's $14.3 billion acquisition of a 49 percent stake in Scale AI in June 2025. Competitors Surge AI and Mercor have likewise seen strong investor demand, backed by their own revenue growth.

data.full_text:
Snorkel AI, a San Francisco-based company developing advanced data infrastructure for artificial intelligence, has raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation in a financing round co-led by Insight Partners and S32. Existing investor Addition also participated significantly. The funding will support the expansion of Snorkel’s agentic data factory, which supplies the specialized datasets, environments, and evaluation frameworks used to train and assess increasingly sophisticated AI systems.

New investors in the round include March Capital, Blumberg Capital, Allegis Capital, Frontline, Standard, and Third Point Ventures.

Existing investors Greylock, Lightspeed, GV, Factory, Prosperity7, Walden Catalyst, and Wells Fargo also participated.

Snorkel plans to use the financing to increase its capacity to serve leading AI laboratories and enterprises while extending its research and technology into additional industries, AI modalities, and applications.

Founded in 2019 out of the Stanford AI Lab, Snorkel develops tools and services for building the specialized data required to improve advanced AI systems.

The company is expanding beyond conventional data labeling, which typically involves assigning categories or other relatively simple annotations to existing information.

Its newer offerings focus on what Snorkel describes as Data 2.0, an approach designed for advanced and agentic AI models that must complete complex, multistep tasks.

These systems require sophisticated training and evaluation materials, including realistic task environments, expert-developed instructions, and detailed assessment criteria.

Creating such materials can take highly qualified specialists hours or days, particularly in industries where accurate outcomes depend on substantial professional knowledge.

Snorkel’s agentic data factory combines expert human involvement with proprietary technology to produce these research-grade datasets and evaluation environments at greater scale.

The company works with leading AI laboratories and enterprises on data used for frontier model training, evaluation, and performance measurement.

Its expert Data-as-a-Service offering, launched in September 2025, addresses the growing demand for specialized data development among organizations building advanced AI systems.

Snorkel intends to expand this business into additional high-value sectors, including healthcare, law, and software engineering.

These industries require AI systems to perform complex tasks involving specialized knowledge, detailed reasoning, and accurate responses to information that may evolve throughout a workflow.

The new funding will also support development of Snorkel’s core research capabilities and enable the company to expand into additional types of data and model architectures.

Snorkel’s founding team has made extensive contributions to data-centric artificial intelligence. According to the company, its research includes more than 250 peer-reviewed papers with over 25,000 citations.

The company plans to continue supporting open research through initiatives such as its Open Benchmarks Grants program, which encourages the development of publicly available AI evaluation resources.

The financing provides additional resources as Snorkel expands its role in the development of training and evaluation infrastructure for frontier and enterprise AI.

“Snorkel’s research-grade approach to AI data, environments, and measurement is becoming an increasingly important ingredient in building capable and reliable AI systems – and their demonstrated growth at scale reflects that. We’re excited to back Alex and the team as they continue to bring their frontier AI data factory capabilities to longer-running, complex work in high value industries like healthcare, law, and software engineering.”

Lonne Jaffe, Managing Director at Insight Partners

“Snorkel’s expert-agentic environments create a unique flywheel between human expertise and AI, delivering data at the speed and quality that enables a new era of efficiency and accuracy for model development. Working with Snorkel ensures the highest frontier model success rate and creates a true partnership between model developer and data provider.”

Andy Harrison, CEO and General Partner of S32

data.title: Snorkel AI Triples Valuation to $3.5B on Training Data Demand
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million in Series E funding on September 22, tripling its valuation to $3.5 billion. The data startup's annualized revenue run rate is $375 million, an eighteenfold increase over the past year. The company pivoted to data-as-a-service, combining synthetic data with expert contributions.
data.author: Abdul Wasay
data.full_text:
Snorkel AI raised $350 million in Series E funding on September 22. The data startup tripled its valuation to $3.5 billion in just seventeen months. This remarkable growth reflects an urgent crisis consuming the AI industry globally. Frontier models now hunger for training data faster than companies can provide it.

Insight Partners and S32 led the round alongside existing investors Addition, Lightspeed, Greylock, GV, and Wells Fargo. The seven-year-old startup originally provided software automating manual data labeling tasks. However, Snorkel shifted strategy last year toward data-as-a-service, delivering completed datasets directly. This pivot proved transformative for company growth and margins significantly.

The hybrid approach combines synthetic data generated by Snorkel’s models with subject matter expert contributions. This strategy differs fundamentally from pure human labor marketplaces operating today. Snorkel’s annualized revenue run rate now stands at $375 million. This represents an eighteenfold increase over the previous twelve months alone. Such explosive growth underscores how desperately AI labs need training data access.

Competing data companies are experiencing similar trajectories now. Mercor achieved $2 billion in gross annualized revenue. Handshake crossed the $1 billion milestone earlier this year. Micro1 scaled to $500 million gross run rate recently.

However, these figures merit careful interpretation because these companies pay 60-70% directly to domain specialists doing the work. Snorkel operates differently through its hybrid model structure. Its payments to human experts land in cost of goods sold rather than inflating headline revenue metrics.

CEO Alex Ratner co-founded Snorkel following four years researching at Stanford’s AI lab. The company launched commercially in 2019 with this academic foundation. Since then, Snorkel built deep relationships with major AI labs and corporations worldwide.

As frontier models scale toward trillion-parameter scales, training data demand grows exponentially. Snorkel positioned itself perfectly to capture this expanding opportunity through innovative data strategies.

data.title: Insight Partners, S32 back Snorkel AI at $3.5B valuation with $350M raise — TFN
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly triple its price 17 months ago. Its annualized revenue jumped from about $20 million to over $350 million in a year. The company expects to turn a profit this year.
data.author: Abhinaya Prabhu
data.full_text:
- Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly triple its price 17 months ago.
- Its annualised revenue jumped from roughly $20 million to more than $350 million in a year.
- The round underlines a broader shift: AI labs now pay for finished, expert-built data.
Snorkel AI just got a lot more expensive, and it’s not because it labels data faster than anyone else anymore. The company, which used to sell software for tagging training data, now builds and sells the finished datasets and simulated work environments that frontier labs train their models on.
That pivot has taken its annualised revenue from around $20 million a year ago to more than $350 million now, and investors have responded by tripling its valuation to $3.5 billion in a $350 million round.
Insight Partners and S32 co-led the raise, with existing backers Addition, Greylock, Wells Fargo, Lightspeed, GV and several others returning, alongside new investors including March Capital and Third Point Ventures. It brings Snorkel to nearly three times the $1.3 billion valuation it held after its $100 million round in May 2025.
From labelling software to a data factory
Snorkel was founded in 2019 by Alex Ratner, Chris Ré, Paroma Varma, Braden Hancock and Henry Ehrenberg, spinning out of Stanford’s AI Lab, where Ratner and Ré had built the original open-source Snorkel project. For years, the company sold tools that let enterprises label their own data.
Since launching a data-as-a-service business in September 2025, it has flipped that model: human specialists across coding, law and medicine now design tasks and grading rubrics, while a layer of AI models automates quality control, producing datasets and reinforcement-learning environments it sells directly to labs, hyperscalers, enterprises and the US federal government.
“Our strong view is that 100% of the data that labs will get value out of will have some human input in the foreseeable future. But 100% of that data will have to use synthetic and automated approaches to keep up with this complexity ,” said Ratner.
The data race is getting more competitive
Snorkel isn’t the only one cashing in on labs running out of usable internet text. Scale AI raised $1 billion at close to a $14 billion valuation before Meta later bought a 49% stake worth roughly $14.3 billion. Mercor went from a $30 million seed round to a $10 billion valuation on a similar bet, and has since been in talks to double that again. Surge AI, meanwhile, was reportedly weighing a first-ever outside raise at north of $25 billion.
Snorkel’s pitch against that crowd is that it designs the tasks and grades the output, which is a harder thing to compete away on price.
Snorkel says the capital will fund more researchers and engineers, expand its enterprise and government business, support third-party model evaluations, and push into new industries and data formats. It expects to turn a profit this year.
“Data is becoming more rare, more specialized, more difficult to find. If you want to train the most frontier, complex and capable models, now you need superior data,” said Andy Harrison, partner at S32 who co-led the funding.
If the last 18 months were about labs discovering they’d run out of internet to scrape, the next stretch is about who gets paid to manufacture what’s missing. Snorkel just put $3.5 billion that it can be the one doing the manufacturing — the harder question is whether that job stays defensible once every well-funded rival is building the same expert-plus-AI pitch.

data.full_text:
Training data provider Snorkel AI raises $350M at $3.5B valuation
Snorkel AI Inc., a provider of artificial intelligence training data, today disclosed that it has raised $350 million in funding.
Insight and S32 led the Series E deal. They were joined by more than a half-dozen other backers including Alphabet Inc.’s GV startup fund.
Snorkel AI was founded in 2019 by researchers from the Stanford AI Lab. Its first product was Snorkel Flow, a software platform that reduced the amount of work involved in supervised learning projects. Supervised learning is an AI development method that trains neural networks using labeled datasets. Such files comprise prompts and correct, human-generated answers to those prompts.
Creating labeled datasets is a highly time-consuming process. Snorkel Flow automated the process using statistical methods developed by the company’s founders at Stanford. According to Snorkel AI, those methods addressed the accuracy issues that made earlier automation approaches ineffective.
Last year, the company changed its business model. It pivoted from selling software that helps developers create training data to providing ready-to-use training datasets. Additionally, Snorkel AI expanded its focus beyond supervised learning to a second, more complex AI training approach known as reinforcement learning.
Whereas supervised learning uses datasets that contain prompts and correct answers to those prompts, reinforcement learning datasets contain unanswered questions. The AI model being trained must figure how to answer them without any human assistance. Once it produces a response, human reviewers or an automated system verify its accuracy. They then provide the AI with feedback that helps improve its reasoning.
Snorkel AI relies on tens of thousands of human experts to generate reinforcement learning training tasks. The company also provides customers with other technical assets that are needed for AI training runs.
When an AI model completes a reinforcement learning task, human reviewers check its work based on predefined evaluation criteria. Those criteria can span several pages. In the case of a programming task, for example, the evaluation guidance must cover all the cybersecurity and performance requirements that AI-generated code must meet.
Snorkel AI develops AI evaluation rubrics for customers. Furthermore, it improves those rubrics over time based on feedback from the human AI reviewers who use them. Some of that feedback is generated when two human reviewers give different scores to an AI prompt response. Such differences usually point to an inconsistency in the underlying evaluation criteria.
AI models are often trained in specialized virtual environments. A code generation model, for example, might require a simulated version of a developer workstation. Snorkel AI provides such as training sandboxes alongside its datasets and evaluation rubrics.
“Since launching our new data-as-a-service offering nearly a year ago, we’ve grown over 18 times, and this week crossed an annualized revenue run rate of $375 million,” co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Alex Ratner detailed in a blog post.
The company will reportedly use its newly raised funding to hire more engineers. Snorkel AI also plans to invest in AI safety initiatives and support the development of open-source model evaluation benchmarks.

data.title: The pivot behind Snorkel AI's $3.5 billion valuation
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly tripling its May 2025 valuation. Its annualized revenue run-rate crossed $350 million, up from about $20 million a year earlier, after pivoting to data-as-a-service. The company expects to reach profitability this year, but renewal risk remains.
data.author: Anders Mirofollow
data.full_text:
The headline number hides the one that matters. Snorkel AI, a Redwood City data startup spun out of the Stanford AI lab, raised $350 million in fresh funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, nearly triple the $1.3 billion valuation investors set in May 2025. But the figure underneath is the striking one: its annualized revenue run-rate crossed $350 million this year, up from roughly $20 million a year earlier. A company does not grow like that by doing more of the same. It grew like that by changing what it sells.

For most of its life, Snorkel sold software861053--. Its programmatic labeling tools — which let a data team turn an expert's rules into training data instead of hand-annotating every example — built a respectable enterprise business and, in May 2025, a $100 million round led by Addition. Then, in September 2025, it added a "data-as-a-service" offering: finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, sold as products rather than as a tool to build them. That pivot is the entire story of the tripling. What changed is not just the growth rate but what the revenue line measures and who pays for it.

The new customers are the most concentrated, best-capitalized buyers in technology: frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, enterprises, and the U.S. federal government. Demand has centered on coding data, with law and medicine behind it. To produce it, Snorkel draws on a network of tens of thousands of specialists in those fields, working alongside a fleet of specialized AI agents.

Here is where a careful reader should slow down, because one accounting choice does real work. Snorkel does not charge customers for human labor. It sells the finished data, and payments to its experts sit in cost of goods sold — below the revenue line. Its $350 million run-rate is therefore a top-line figure: that largest cost is recorded as an expense below the revenue line, not subtracted from the headline number. Not every rival reports it that way: the pass-through competitors in this space hand 60% to 70% of their top-line income to outside specialists, so a same-sized gross number from one of them overstates how much value it keeps. This is part of why Snorkel expects to reach profitability this year even while growing this fast.

The catch is that it is still a services business, and a services business captures value only as long as the customer keeps buying. The cleanliness of the accounting does not tell you whether a frontier lab will renew at these prices a year from now — whether Snorkel's data measurably improves its models, or whether a customer worth tens of billions decides it would rather own the capability. That last risk is live. Meta's June 2025 purchase of a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.3 billion shows how high the data bottleneck has risen, and how willing the biggest AI spenders are to buy their way into it. The concentration that makes Snorkel's customers rich enough to pay also makes them powerful enough to internalize the work or fund a competitor.

Work through the arithmetic and the round looks ordinary for the category. A $3.5 billion valuation against a $350 million run-rate is roughly ten times revenue, unremarkable for a hypergrowth AI infrastructureAIIA-- name. The valuation tripled not because ten times became extraordinary but because the revenue in the denominator grew about seventeenfold in a year. An investor's honest question is not whether the multiple is rich. It is whether the revenue is real and repeatable. It is real in that customers pay for finished data. Its repeatability is unproved, because a year-old services run-rate sold to a handful of hyperconcentrated buyers has not yet been tested through a single renewal cycle.

The round is a signal about the AI stack even for investors who will never own a share of Snorkel. Value has been sliding from raw compute toward the data that decides how good a model actually is, and a company that spent years as a modest labeling tool just converted that position into more than $350 million of annualized revenue in a year. The bullish case is a flywheel — human expertise training specialized agents that make the next dataset cheaper and better, so each renewal gets harder to walk away from. The case that fails it is a services business whose revenue rests on a few laboratories that could, at sufficient scale, build the capability themselves. What separates the two is not the tripled valuation but the one thing nine months of new revenue cannot yet show: whether the customers come back.

data.title: Snorkel AI's $3.5 Billion Round Looked Like a Re-Rating — It Was Actually a Discount
data.ai_summary: Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, co-led by Insight Partners and S32. The company's annualized revenue crossed $350 million, down from $20 million a year prior, making the round a discount on sales. It expects to reach profitability this year.
data.author: Julian Cruzfollow
data.full_text:
After the close on Monday, private AI data company Snorkel AI said it had raised $350 million in fresh funding at a $3.5 billion valuation, in a round co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with existing investors Addition, Greylock and Wells Fargo participating.

On its face that reads like a startup in escape velocity — nearly three times the $1.3 billion Snorkel fetched in its May 2025 round. But the more revealing math sits underneath, because on a sales basis the company actually got cheaper.

Here is the ledger. Annualized revenue has crossed $350 million, up from approximately $20 million a year prior. Divide today's $3.5 billion valuation by that roughly $350 million run-rate and you get about 10 times sales. Run the same divide on the May 2025 round — $1.3 billion on roughly $20 million of revenue — and you're at about 65 times. In absolute dollars the company nearly tripled in value; on revenue it de-rated by a factor of more than six. That is not the shape of a bubble round. It's the shape of a company that grew into its number.

The reason the number moved so fast is that the business itself changed. Snorkel was founded in 2019 by Stanford AI lab researchers and built its name on software861053-- — Snorkel Flow, a programmatic data-labeling platform. For years that software model produced only modest revenue. Then, in September 2025, the company launched a data-as-a-service business: instead of selling tools, it began selling finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments, and it sells the resulting data products rather than charging for human labor.

The pivot was a genuine break, not a cosmetic one. Right around that same launch, Snorkel cut 31 of about 240 employees — roughly 13% of the workforce — with software engineers hit hardest, as the company said it was deprioritizing legacy areas. You don't lay off your software engineers the month after launching the product you were built around unless the old model wasn't scaling. The layoff and the launch describe the same event from two directions.

All of which points at the question that matters for anyone sizing the AI data theme: is this data-as-a-service a product, or a services business in disguise? The bull case is that it leans toward product. Snorkel combines teams of human experts in coding, law and medicine with specialized AI models and agents for quality control, then sells the finished data; it does not bill for headcount. Cost it favorably and that could carry software-like margins, and Reuters reports the company expects to reach profitability this year.

The bear case is that any business built around expert humans carries heavier costs than a pure software license, and the public AI complex makes that tension visible. PalantirPLTR--, the closest big public AI software name, trades at roughly 72 times trailing sales with a gross margin near 85%, as of Monday's close. Against that, Snorkel at about 10 times forward run-rate looks cheap — but Palantir sells software and Snorkel sells data with a human-expert layer inside it. A discount to 72 times sales doesn't automatically mean fair value if the cost structure never reaches software margins. The whole gap between Snorkel's single-digit multiple and Palantir's 70-plus is a wager on how productized, and how margin-rich, "expert data" can actually get.

For an ordinary retail reader, the honest caveat is that you cannot buy Snorkel — it is privately held, and none of this re-rating is capturable in a brokerage account. What the round is, then, is a live data point on the AI supply chain: the market increasingly treats high-quality training and evaluation data as the binding constraint on frontier models, and it is willing to pay for the companies that produce it. The public way to express that bet runs through the AI software names, which already carry far richer multiples — so a private raise at about 10 times run-rate either validates the theme or is a reminder of how extended the public AI complex has become. It can be both.

When I rank the live issues here, valuation is not the one that worries me. At roughly 10 times a growing, near-breakeven run-rate, the price looks defensible even if the dollar figure in the headline is big. The larger question is the durability and the margins of the data-as-a-service model, which is barely a year old and, by the company's own accounting, only just approaching profitability. I'd take the round as real evidence that the AI data layer is a competitive bottleneck worth watching, but I'd want to see proof that a human-expert data business can hold software-like margins across a few more quarters of scale before giving it the benefit of the doubt. Profitability is expected this year, not yet delivered.

If the run rate keeps compounding at these margins, a roughly 10x multiple has organic support; if growth decelerates sharply or a major customer pulls the work inside, there is no public bid standing by to catch the price. The open question is not whether Snorkel deserves more per dollar of sales than it did a year ago — it clearly does — but whether the data-as-a-service compound can keep clearing past $350 million and, eventually, at what price a public market chooses to value it. The headline capital includes $240 million non-dilutive financing from Heidi, leaving roughly $1.139 billion in equity. Investors are concentrating capital on companies controlling strategic bottlenecks in AI infrastructure.

Venture capital today is clustering around a surprisingly consistent idea: the next layer of AI value is shifting away from the model itself and toward the systems that make AI usable, governable, trustworthy, and economically productive. Cybersecurity company Cyera pulled in another $400 million. Snorkel AI raised $350 million to supply increasingly specialized training data and reinforcement-learning environments. Heidi Health paired a $100 million equity round with a $240 million non-dilutive facility as clinical AI moves from transcription into healthcare workflows. That pattern continues further down the funding stack. Go.AI is putting private AI infrastructure inside regulated institutions. Firecrawl is building the data-access layer agents need to interact with the web. Baselayer is attacking financial fraud. Sela is applying voice agents specifically to mortgage sales, while Teal Health and Ramona Optics show that investors are still willing to finance differentiated healthcare and life-science infrastructure outside the generative-AI rush. Axios’ deal reporting captures the unusually dense cluster of enterprise AI, security, fintech and healthcare rounds announced Tuesday. Across the ten rounds selected below, the headline capital committed totals about $1.379 billion. That figure needs one qualification: $240 million of Heidi’s package is non-dilutive financing rather than equity, leaving roughly $1.139 billion of equity or equity-like venture/growth funding in the selected set. The three largest transactions, Cyera, Snorkel AI, and Heidi, account for about 79% of headline capital, or roughly three-quarters of the equity component. That concentration is the day’s clearest market signal: investors are writing very large checks where companies can demonstrate strategic control points, customer adoption or both. The Macro Environment: Capital Is Paying for Control, Not Just Intelligence The backdrop is not one of cheap money. The Federal Reserve raised its target range by 25 basis points on September 16 to 3.75%–4.00%, meaning venture investors are still competing against a meaningful cost of capital. That makes today’s nine-figure private rounds more revealing than they would be in a zero-rate environment: investors are reserving large checks for businesses they believe can either dominate a category or become infrastructure other businesses cannot easily remove. Cyera is a good example of the first category. Goldman Sachs is putting $400 million into a company already valued at more than $12 billion, shortly after Cyera completed its $1 billion acquisition of non-human-identity specialist Oasis Security. The investment is less about financing basic product development than giving Cyera enough balance-sheet latitude to broaden its platform, pursue federal and overseas customers, make acquisitions, and choose its own timing for a future public offering. The Wall Street Journal reports that Cyera has raised $1.94 billion since June 2025 alone and has now landed its first customer spending more than $10 million annually. Snorkel represents the second category: infrastructure underneath increasingly capable models. Its annualized revenue run-rate has risen from roughly $20 million a year ago to more than $350 million, according to Reuters, as frontier labs need harder training tasks, specialist-generated datasets and reinforcement-learning environments rather than commodity labeling. At a $3.5 billion valuation, the round prices Snorkel at roughly ten times its reported annualized revenue — a valuation that looks aggressive in ordinary software but much less unusual for a company growing at this speed and positioning itself directly in the frontier-model supply chain. We calculated that multiple from Reuters’ reported valuation and revenue figures. Private and public capital are also beginning to meet around AI infrastructure. On the same day these venture rounds surfaced, data-center infrastructure provider Accelevation set U.S. IPO terms at $20 to $24 per share, implying a market capitalization of around $4.9 billion at the midpoint. That does not mean the public market is broadly open to every venture-backed software company. It suggests something narrower: businesses connected to AI’s physical, security, and operational requirements have a more credible path toward institutional-scale financing than undifferentiated application companies. The implication for founders is important. Calling a product “AI-native” is not enough to command premium capital. Today’s stronger financings sit at specific bottlenecks: who can access sensitive data, where models run, how training data is generated, how clinical work is documented, how agents retrieve information, and how regulated transactions are verified. Investors appear increasingly willing to fund the companies that own those bottlenecks rather than another thin interface sitting on top of somebody else’s model. The Top Funding Rounds Cyera raises $400M to secure data and AI-agent access across the enterprise Cyera’s $400 million investment from Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives extends the company’s Series G and comes only months after a $600 million Series G valued the New York cybersecurity company at $12 billion. Cyera says the new investment will support its AI-security roadmap, federal-market expansion and continued growth across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific. The strategic premise has broadened substantially from classic data-security posture management. Enterprises deploying AI agents now have software identities that can call tools, query databases, and act on corporate information without constant human involvement. Cyera’s acquisition of Oasis Security brought non-human identity management into the same platform as data security, allowing the company to address both sides of the permission problem: where sensitive information sits and which human, machine or agent can reach it. That is also why Goldman entering at this stage is notable. This is late-stage capital going into a company that already has the scale to contemplate an IPO, not a speculative bet on whether a category will exist. The Wall Street Journal reports that Cyera’s newest financing gives it additional freedom to invest in products and M&A while delaying a listing if private capital remains attractive. For competing data-security and identity vendors, that creates a well-funded consolidator with both an acquisition currency and a $12 billion-plus valuation benchmark. Funding Details

Investors: Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives; existing Series G was led by Evolution Equity

Amount Raised: $400 million

Total Raised: Approximately $2.7 billion reported overall; $1.94 billion raised since June 2025

Funding Stage: Series G extension

Funding Date: September 22, 2026

Headquarters: New York, New York, U.S.

Sector: Cybersecurity, data security, AI-agent security, identity security Snorkel AI raises $350M to become the data infrastructure behind frontier AI Snorkel AI raised $350 million at a $3.5 billion valuation, co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with participation from Greylock and Wells Fargo. The valuation is almost three times the $1.3 billion figure attached to Snorkel’s $100 million financing in May 2025. More striking is the operating trajectory: Reuters reports annualized revenue above $350 million, versus roughly $20 million a year earlier. The change is tied to a strategic pivot. Snorkel began as software for programmatic data labeling but has increasingly become a supplier of finished datasets and reinforcement-learning environments. Its network includes specialists in coding, law and medicine, while AI systems automate portions of quality assurance and data production. CEO Alex Ratner argues that increasingly capable models require data that is harder to source and judge, creating demand for human expertise combined with automated production rather than conventional annotation labor. That places Snorkel in a market reshaped by Scale AI, Mercor, Surge AI and the frontier labs’ appetite for difficult training and evaluation data. Reuters notes that investor interest intensified after Meta’s 2025 purchase of a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.3 billion. Snorkel’s answer is to sell the data product rather than bill customers for hours of human work — potentially giving it better operating leverage if it can preserve quality as volumes rise. The company says it expects to reach profitability this year, an unusually consequential detail for a company growing this quickly. Funding Details

Sector: AI training data, reinforcement learning, model evaluation infrastructure Heidi Health raises $100M in equity and secures a $240M growth facility for clinical AI Heidi Health’s financing is best understood as $100 million of Series C equity plus a $240 million non-dilutive growth facility, not a conventional $340 million venture round. Blackbird led the equity financing, with Phoenix Court and, according to Axios, Point72 Private Investments and Headline participating; General Catalyst led the $240 million financing component. The Melbourne healthtech startup started with an AI medical scribe but is pushing toward a broader clinical-workflow platform. The Times reports that Heidi handles about 2.8 million patient interactions each week in 110 languages and has won a major NHS clinical documentation deployment spanning 15 trusts and integrated-care organizations, as well as more than 1,200 GP practices in England’s Midlands. That moves the thesis beyond whether clinicians will use an ambient scribe: the harder question is whether one vendor can become part of the operating layer of large health systems. Valuation reporting differs slightly by outlet. The Times puts the latest valuation at about $900 million, while Australian coverage describes Heidi as reaching roughly the $1 billion or unicorn threshold. The discrepancy likely reflects rounding and reporting conventions, not two separate financings. The more important signal is the financing structure itself. Using $240 million of non-dilutive capital lets Heidi finance expansion without selling the same amount of ownership at today’s valuation — a playbook increasingly relevant to rapidly growing software companies with enough revenue visibility to support structured capital. Sector: Healthtech, clinical AI, medical documentation and workflow automation Go.AI raises $85M to bring private AI infrastructure inside regulated institutions Chicago-based Go.AI raised an $85 million Series A led by Updata Partners, with existing investors GFT Ventures and LAUNCH participating. The financing puts the company’s total capital raised at roughly $90 million. Go.AI sells AI hardware appliances aimed particularly at banks and other regulated organizations that cannot casually move confidential data or sensitive workloads into external AI services. That makes this an infrastructure bet rather than another model-company wager. Banks increasingly want access to generative AI while preserving control over data residency, audit trails, security, and deployment architecture. Go.AI is trying to occupy the gap between public AI APIs and a fully bespoke internal stack by packaging compute and software into systems that institutions can run under their own governance. Competitive pressure will come from both directions: hyperscalers can offer private-cloud configurations, while server, chip, and enterprise-software companies can assemble their own on-premises AI stacks. Go.AI therefore has to win on deployment speed, regulatory fit, and operating simplicity rather than raw model capability. The size of the Series A suggests investors believe regulated AI deployment itself can become a meaningful product category. Funding Details

Sector: AI infrastructure, private AI, financial-services technology Firecrawl raises $75M to build the web-data layer for AI agents Firecrawl raised a $75 million Series B led by Smash Capital, with Altos Ventures, Nexus Venture Partners, Y Combinator, Freestyle, and Offline also participating. Axios describes the company as providing data infrastructure for AI agents — the layer that turns information on the open web into material software agents can retrieve and use programmatically. That may sound like plumbing, but plumbing becomes more valuable as agents move beyond chat interfaces. An AI system asked to research companies, monitor competitors, source products, qualify leads, or execute workflows needs fresh external data in a predictable structure. Model vendors can improve reasoning, but they do not automatically solve crawling, extraction, website changes, access reliability or data preparation. This is the deeper reason infrastructure investors continue financing companies around the model layer. As foundation models become easier to substitute, the differentiated asset can move to the systems that supply them with current information and connect them to real-world workflows. Firecrawl still faces a crowded field spanning web search, crawling, browser automation, and structured-data extraction, so its long-term position will depend on whether developers treat it as a default component rather than one interchangeable API among many. Sector: Developer infrastructure, web data, AI-agent infrastructure Baselayer raises $35M to make financial fraud detection an infrastructure layer Baselayer raised $35 million in Series A financing led by M13, with Picus Capital, Afore Capital and Torch Capital participating. The company provides fraud-detection technology to banks and other financial institutions, a category gaining importance as automated account creation, synthetic identities and increasingly capable software systems make old verification processes harder to rely on. Investors are effectively betting on a second-order effect of AI adoption. More automation doesn’t just create opportunities for productivity software; it increases the volume and sophistication of activity that financial institutions must authenticate. That creates demand for infrastructure that can assess counterparties and suspicious behavior without adding manual review to every transaction. Baselayer’s challenge is that fraud, KYC, and identity verification already contain well-funded incumbents. Its opportunity is to build for a world in which the entity on the other side of a workflow may increasingly be software rather than a person. Even without assuming that every AI agent will need a separate financial identity, the sheer increase in machine-mediated transactions should raise the value of higher-frequency verification. The company is building an AI platform for in-house legal teams, placing it in one of the most heavily financed vertical-AI categories outside healthcare. Legal software is an instructive test of where AI application companies can retain pricing power. General-purpose models can draft and summarize text increasingly well, which puts pressure on products whose only differentiation is a legal-themed interface. Defensibility has to come from workflow integration, permissioning, institutional knowledge, matter history, review systems and the ability to fit into how corporate legal departments actually operate. That explains why specialist platforms can still command venture backing even as foundational capabilities improve. Legal departments do not buy model tokens; they buy reduced outside-counsel spend, faster contract and matter handling, and a defensible process for sensitive corporate work. Chamelio’s opportunity is therefore less about having a uniquely intelligent model and more about owning enough of the legal workflow that switching products becomes costly. Funding Details

Sector: Legal technology, enterprise AI Ramona Optics raises $25M to scale high-throughput microscopy Durham, North Carolina-based Ramona Optics raised a $25 million Series A led by ARCH Venture Partners, with Stealthpoint Ventures and ND Capital participating. Founded in 2016 by two Caltech graduate students before relocating to Durham, the company makes advanced microscopes designed to increase the scale and speed of biological sample analysis. This is one of the day’s more interesting non-generative-AI transactions because it addresses the physical side of biological data generation. Better computational biology does not remove the need to capture high-quality experimental information in the first place. If laboratories can image larger sample areas or run experiments faster, the downstream value flows into drug discovery, cellular biology and increasingly automated research workflows. ARCH Venture Partners’ involvement is notable because the firm’s life-science investing history places a high bar on whether a scientific tool can become more than laboratory equipment. Teal is developing a self-collection system for at-home HPV-based cervical-cancer screening, shifting a procedure historically associated with an in-clinic visit toward a consumer-accessible workflow. The venture thesis is not simply “healthcare at home.” Screening businesses work only when the entire path — collection, laboratory processing, clinical interpretation, follow-up and payment — functions together. That creates more execution risk than a pure software product but also creates a stronger barrier if a company can integrate those pieces successfully. Voice generation is becoming cheaper and more widely available, so merely producing natural-sounding speech is unlikely to remain defensible. Vertical products instead need to understand industry terminology, connect with existing systems, handle escalation, operate within compliance requirements, and improve measurable conversion or labor economics. Mortgages are an attractive but demanding proving ground: high customer value supports meaningful software pricing, while the regulated nature of lending raises the cost of inaccurate or uncontrolled automation. Sector: Voice AI, mortgage technology, financial-services automation What Today’s Funding Activity Reveals The first pattern is capital concentration. Roughly four-fifths of the $1.379 billion in headline financing represented here went into Cyera, Snorkel, and Heidi. On an equity-only basis after stripping out Heidi’s $240 million non-dilutive facility, those three still account for roughly 75% of the selected capital. Investors are not spreading money evenly across the AI economy. They are concentrating it around companies with evidence of category leadership, unusually high growth, or strategically scarce infrastructure. The second pattern is that AI infrastructure has expanded beyond GPUs and data centers. Today’s deals define infrastructure much more broadly: Snorkel supplies the training and evaluation data; Firecrawl supplies external information to agents; Go.AI supplies controlled deployment environments; Cyera controls sensitive-data access; Baselayer addresses trust and fraud. Taken together, these financings suggest the investable AI stack is moving outward from compute into governance, context, verification and deployment. Third, vertical AI is being held to a different standard than it was two years ago. Heidi, Chamelio and Sela are not being financed merely because they insert a language model into healthcare, legal or lending workflows. Their investment cases increasingly depend on owning the surrounding process. In healthcare, that means integration with clinical systems and institutional deployment; in legal, it means privileged organizational context and workflow; in mortgages, it means compliance and conversion economics. Fourth, cybersecurity is becoming a direct beneficiary of agent adoption rather than a separate technology category. Cyera’s strategy of combining data governance with non-human identity management reflects a broader issue: autonomous software can only become more useful by receiving more permissions. Every additional permission creates another security decision. The value of the agent and the value of controlling the agent may therefore rise together. Cyera’s $12 billion-plus valuation is one of the strongest private-market expressions of that thesis so far. Finally, geography is more concentrated than the word “global” might imply in this particular 12-hour slice. The United States dominates the selected rounds, with Australia represented by Heidi and cross-border capital visible throughout the investor syndicates. That should not be read as evidence that European or emerging-market funding disappeared Tuesday: several sizable European and international deals surfaced in September 22 newsletters but traced back to September 21 or outside the strict cutoff and were therefore removed from this edition. Comparative Funding Table Startup Amount Raised Sector Funding Stage Lead Investors Country Cyera $400M Cybersecurity / AI security Series G extension Goldman Sachs Alternatives U.S. Snorkel AI $350M AI data / RL infrastructure Growth round Insight Partners, S32 U.S. Heidi Health $340M package ($100M equity + $240M facility) Clinical AI Series C + non-dilutive financing Blackbird; General Catalyst on facility Australia Go.AI $85M Private AI infrastructure Series A Updata Partners U.S. Firecrawl $75M AI-agent / web-data infrastructure Series B Smash Capital U.S. Baselayer $35M Fraud / financial infrastructure Series A M13 U.S. Chamelio $26M Legal AI Series A Entrée Capital U.S./Israel Ramona Optics $25M Life-science tools Series A ARCH Venture Partners U.S. Teal Health $22M Women’s health/diagnostics Series A .406 Ventures U.S. Sela $21M Voice AI/mortgage tech Seed + Series A Emergence Capital, Costanoa U.S. The table also shows why round size alone can mislead. Heidi’s headline $340 million is not economically equivalent to Snorkel’s $350 million financing because $240 million of Heidi’s package is non-dilutive. Likewise, Cyera’s $400 million arrives at a $12 billion-plus valuation and late-stage scale, while a $21 million check into Sela carries far more ownership and company-building significance at an earlier stage. Comparing venture rounds requires looking at capital structure, stage and strategic intent, not only the number in the headline. Strategic Takeaways for Founders and Investors For founders, the bar for “AI differentiation” is moving up quickly. Access to a capable model is becoming less persuasive as a fundraising story. Today’s financings reward companies that can explain what they control around the model: proprietary data production, regulated distribution, embedded workflow, identity and permissions, deployment architecture, physical instrumentation, or institutional relationships. Firecrawl, Snorkel, and Go.AI occupy different layers, but all three sell something the underlying model does not provide on its own. The best vertical-AI businesses are becoming workflow businesses. Founders should therefore measure outcomes that buyers actually budget for: clinician hours returned, mortgage conversion rates, legal work brought in-house, fraud losses reduced or deployment time shortened. A company whose value proposition collapses when inference prices fall faces commoditization. A company whose product gets more valuable as models get cheaper has a much stronger economic position. Treat security and governance as product surfaces, not compliance afterthoughts. Cyera’s financing shows how large the market can become when AI adoption creates a new class of access-control problem. For enterprise founders, the ability to explain what an agent can see, which tools it can call, and how its actions are audited may become part of the sales proposition rather than a box checked after deployment. Capital structure is becoming part of competitive strategy. Heidi’s combination of $100 million in equity with a $240 million non-dilutive facility is especially instructive. Companies with substantial revenue and predictable expansion requirements do not always need to fund every growth dollar by selling shares. Debt, structured facilities and other non-dilutive instruments can preserve founder and employee ownership — provided the business has the cash-generation profile to carry the obligation. Late-stage investors are paying for option value. Goldman Sachs’ investment in Cyera gives the company additional time before an IPO, more acquisition capacity and greater flexibility in deciding when to access public markets. For mature private companies, a strong balance sheet can therefore become competitive weaponry: it reduces pressure to list at an inconvenient moment and can turn the company into an acquirer while weaker competitors are still conserving cash. Investors, meanwhile, need to distinguish real infrastructure from temporary abstraction layers. Some AI tooling categories will be absorbed by model providers, cloud platforms or larger enterprise-software vendors. The stronger bets are likely to be products whose value grows with AI usage but whose function is difficult for a model provider to internalize: access governance, specialized proprietary data, regulated deployment, physical data generation and deeply integrated industry workflows. The biggest pricing risk is at the application layer. If two products use similar foundation models, operate on the same customer data and connect to the same systems, switching costs can deteriorate quickly. The financing environment is therefore increasingly rewarding companies that can answer a hard question with specificity: what becomes harder for a customer to replace as your company gets bigger? Conclusion September 22’s funding activity is not simply another day in which “AI got most of the money.” The more useful interpretation is that venture capital is becoming more discriminating about which parts of the AI economy deserve durable margins. Cyera is being financed because autonomous software makes data and identity control harder. Snorkel is being financed because better models require harder-to-produce training and evaluation data. Go.AI is addressing institutions that cannot simply push sensitive workloads into public AI services. Firecrawl addresses the problem of giving agents dependable external information. Heidi, Chamelio and Sela are attempting to turn general AI capability into industry-specific operating systems. Meanwhile, Ramona Optics and Teal Health show that differentiated physical and healthcare products can still draw serious institutional capital without competing in the foundation-model race. The day’s capital concentration matters just as much as the sector mix. With close to four-fifths of headline commitments going to three companies, the market is not behaving like an indiscriminate technology boom. It is behaving like a market willing to pay extraordinary prices for a small number of perceived control points while forcing everyone else to prove the economics at Series A and Series B. That is the signal founders and investors should carry forward. As model intelligence becomes more abundant, scarcity migrates elsewhere: toward trusted data, permissioning, distribution, regulated deployment, specialized workflows, and physical systems that generate information the digital world cannot manufacture by itself. The next valuable startup may still use the same models as everyone else. What matters is whether it owns something around those models that everyone else still needs. 0 Shares

#United States #San Francisco #Insight Partners #Snorkel AI #Data Factory Snorkel AI Secures $350 Million to Advance Frontiers in AI Data Development On September 22, 2026, Snorkel AI, a pivotal player in frontier AI development, announced a significant funding milestone of $350 million, which elevates its valuation to $3.5 billion. This funding round was co-led by Insight Partners and S32, with noteworthy participation from various existing and new investors, including Addition, March Capital, Blumberg Capital, Allegis Capital, and several others. The capital raise underscores Snorkel’s trajectory toward expanding its agentic data factory, which is responsible for producing the underlying data and environments that fuel advanced AI labs globally.



The broader landscape of AI data is witnessing a fundamental shift. In prior eras, developing AI was largely about managing labeling tasks with a workforce-driven approach. However, today’s complex frontier systems demand far more sophisticated capabilities—termed Data 2.0—which entail handling expert tasks that often take skilled human workers days to accomplish. Designing effective solutions in this context has become a research-intensive endeavor, where quality and complexity are critical determinants of value.



To rise to this challenge, Snorkel has established a fresh paradigm for data creation and management. Since launching its Data-as-a-Service platform in September 2025, the company has demonstrated significant growth and relevance in the industry. Partnering with leading AI labs and major enterprises, Snorkel focuses on delivering high-quality data solutions that underpin frontier model evaluation and training processes.



Rooted in the prestigious Stanford AI Lab, which birthed the company nearly a decade ago, Snorkel was founded by a team known for its pioneering work in data-centric AI. This legacy is exemplified by a substantial body of research, including over 250 peer-reviewed papers that collectively have gained more than 25,000 citations.



“The frontier of AI needs research partners who are at the cutting edge of data science,” stated Alex Ratner, co-founder and CEO of Snorkel AI. “Snorkel was designed to be that partner—drawing on over ten years of research and development to be the leading lab for agentic data.”



Lonne Jaffe, Managing Director at Insight Partners, noted, “Snorkel’s rigorous approach to AI data and environments becomes an increasingly critical factor in developing capable and trustworthy AI systems. Their remarkable growth at scale is a testament to the value they deliver.”



According to Andy Harrison, CEO and General Partner at S32, “Snorkel’s unique expert-agentic environments create a synergistic relationship between human skills and AI, offering quality data at unprecedented speeds. This capability enables a new era of efficiency and precision in model development.”



With the fresh funding, Snorkel AI plans to greatly enhance its agentic data factory's capacity to keep pace with demand, strategically invest in vertical and enterprise-level AI solutions, and further its research in new domains and modalities. The company has also committed to enriching its open research initiatives, including the establishment of programs like its Open Benchmarks Grants.



In summary, Snorkel AI’s recent funding round captures the company’s aggressive pursuit of innovation and leadership within the AI landscape, paving the way for its continued contributions to high-performing AI systems for various industries, including healthcare, law, and software engineering.
